Design Dash
Resume

Open-source method

The screen was ready before the team understood it.

I built Design Dash to connect product reasoning to interface decisions. Generating a screen is fast. Knowing what it should do takes more work.

Role
Author and facilitator
Scope
Nine-phase workflow for chats, agents, and workshops
Key decision
One file-based model, with traceable decisions and generated views
Evidence
Used in Renaissance assignment workshops; public method and accepted architecture

I — Inspiration

The files existed. The reasoning was hard to follow.

A prototype can look coherent while the decisions behind it remain scattered across notes and conversations. I built Design Dash around a question the interface alone could not answer: how would a team trace this screen back to the problem and evidence that justified it?

A workshop could produce assumptions, a specification, a flow, a wireframe, and a pitch. Their relationships lived in the prose. To understand why a control existed, someone had to search the folder.

AI made the gap more obvious. A prompt could return cards and filters before the team had named the product’s objects or separated evidence from assumptions. I wanted the workflow to preserve those decisions, not just its outputs.

On the Renaissance Assignments page, I facilitated product and engineering workshops around a shared assignment model. Title, type, assigned date, and due date were common to every assignment. Pages read and questions answered remained product-specific. That distinction gave us a structure we could prototype and test.

D — Design Process

Some decisions needed more review than others

I made the review tier depend on risk, reversibility, and reach. A narrow, reversible change should not require the same process as a regulated workflow. Every tier still has an ethics floor.

Standard work requires evidence, comparison of concepts, reconciliation with the user’s mental model, ethics review, and a learning plan. High-stakes work cannot waive those gates. Simulated reviewers do not count as specialist sign-off.

E — Engagement

Make the model usable in a working session

The Renaissance assignment workshops gave the approach a concrete use. I facilitated sessions with product and engineering around the shared assignment model, while UX research tested the resulting prototypes. People could discuss a product object, see its interface implications, and record unresolved questions in the same working session.

The method had to support that conversation without making a rich document or a particular toolchain compulsory. Keeping a linked file model as the source lets chats and workshops contribute to the same record. The living plan is a generated view, rather than another document everyone has to keep synchronized.

A — Action

A rich document couldn’t be the only way to use the method

An early approach treated a rich living-plan document as the source of truth when a local toolchain was available. That excluded people working in a chat or worksheet and created another summary that could drift.

I accepted a file-based architecture: Markdown records with small headers and typed links form the Dash Model. Chat and workshops write to those records. The Design Plan regenerates from them; a Story freezes a release snapshot. Neither view becomes a second editable source.

I rejected a database as the canonical store because the method needs to work without one. The tradeoff is that the files need explicit validation. An interface must link to a decision, the decision to a requirement or object, and the requirement to an opportunity.

S — Success

The assignment workshops put the method into practice

The Renaissance workshops produced object notes, diagrams, wireframes, and a low-fidelity prototype the team tested. The shipped assignment view came from that shared model.

The workflow is public. The file-based Dash Model is an accepted architecture, with existing dashes moving onto it incrementally. I have no public usage count. The useful test is whether a team can inspect a design decision and find the evidence and product rules behind it.

I’m happy to walk through how the method fits a real product problem.
